In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of sperm storage and the role of sperm competition and sperm chemokinesis in ant queen reproduction.
the evolution of female control over male fertility and its consequences for sperm competition in ants.
the mechanisms by which queens of Acromyremx leaf-cutting ants maximize the reproductive potential of sperm stored for many decades, even though they may mate only once.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sperm chemotaxis is not involved in Acromyrmecin queens, but sperm chemokinesis is.
sperm chemokinesis is a mechanism to enhance the reproductive success of queens.
queen reproductive tract secretions in leaf-cutting ants enhance sperm motility without discriminating between the sperm of related and unrelated males.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the female reproductive tract is an important component of the sperm competition arena in ants.
queen reproductive tract secretions act as a sperm chemoattractant, which enhances the swimming performance of sperm of different males and thereby equalizes the probability of sperm storage.
queen reproductive tract secretions are a key factor that promotes sperm storage success of queens and thus ensures the reproductive success of males.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sperm chemotactic cues can be used to enhance the performance of sperm of all males, not just the best ones.
sperm chemokinetic responses of females may be more common than currently recognized and may play a key role in the evolution of sperm storage strategies.
the queen reproductive tract is an important factor that may determine the success of male reproductive strategies in Acromyrmecine ants, but also in other social insect taxa.
